newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma flexes muscles but showdown unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma flexes muscles but showdown unlikely.

text.p: Russia's opposition-dominated lower house of parliament is flexing its muscles to put pressure on the Kremlin but seems unlikely to push its antagonistic relationship with President Boris Yeltsin to breaking point.

The State Duma tried to sabotage Yeltsin's hopes of rapprochement with Ukraine by seeking a halt to the division of the disputed Black Sea fleet on Wednesday and defying Ukrainian control of the Crimean city of Sevastopol on Thursday.

The Duma has in recent weeks also rejected the government's draft budget, criticised the cabinet's record and savaged a controversial peace agreement for Chechnya. Moves have begun to create a medical commission which would check Yeltsin's health.

But the chamber has strictly limited powers, making its bark worse than its bite. Despite its criticism, Yeltsin's spokesman said all differences over the Black Sea fleet had been resolved at talks on Thursday with Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma.

Communists dominate the Duma and their aim appears to be to show they are a powerful opposition force but without risking an all-out clash which might prompt Yeltsin to dissolve the parliament, as he did to put down a 1993 rebellion by deputies.
"The communists want to push Yeltsin close to the edge but not beyond," Vyacheslav Nikonov, a political analyst who helped plot Yeltsin's re-election last July, told Reuters.

"Most of the communist deputies come from 'nowhere' and getting to Moscow is the peak of their political career. They don't want to risk losing their seats and no one knows how another election would turn out for the communists."
Nikonov, head of the Politika Fund think-tank, said Yeltsin also did not want open confrontation as he prepared for heart surgery next month.

Dissolving the Duma, one of the president's constitutional rights, would risk an even more hostile parliament being elected and the staging of new elections would be costly. "Yeltsin has no intention of dissolving the Duma," Nikonov said.

The Communist Party holds just over one third of the 450 seats in the Duma. The combined opposition, including communists and nationalists, has more than half the seats but is short of the two-thirds needed for some important votes.
Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov has made clear since he lost out to Yeltsin in presidential elections last July that he wants to avoid open conflict, at least for now.

Analysts said he wanted to influence economic policy to benefit the millions of workers he represented and to show he was a responsible and reasonable man who should not be compared with some of his predecessors as communist leaders.
"We will take several conciliatory steps in order to pursue a constructive line," Zyuganov said in a television interview last Sunday.
"The extreme scenario would be bad for everybody...Our experience, dating back many centuries, shows that such extremes tend to have a rather dramatic ending," he said.
Bringing down the government would not necessarily help him. Yeltsin has the right as president to choose the prime minister and dissolve the Duma if it rejects his candidate three times.
Even if new elections were held and the communists made huge gains, Yeltsin would not be obliged to take this into account when forming a government.
The battles being fought look purely tactical, rather than intended to seek decisive victories.
The debate over the draft 1997 budget, to which the Duma has demanded changes, is an annual battle which gives the opposition a platform to attack government economic policy.

The criticism of the peace deal for breakaway Chechnya provided Zyuganov with a chance to attack a potential presidential rival in Alexander Lebed, who signed the agreement but has since been sacked by Yeltsin as his security chief.

Communist proposals for the creation of a medical commission to regularly check the health of state leaders -- a move which could threaten Yeltsin with dismissal on health grounds -- are widely seen as having no chance of being approved.

The Black Sea fleet dispute gave the communists what they regarded as a chance to show voters they were patriots and to match tough recent statements on the fleet by Lebed and Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov, another likely presidential challenger.
